subject: general
question: The Faraizi Movement's no-tax campaign primarily targeted the ________.
solution:
The correct answer is __**Indigo planters and zamindars**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Faraizi Movement** was initiated by **Haji Shariatullah** in the early 19th century in Bengal with the aim of purifying Islam and fighting socio-economic oppression.
 
• One of the core aspects of the movement was the **no-tax campaign**, targeting the oppressive practices of **Indigo planters and zamindars** who exploited peasants.
 
• The Indigo planters were mostly European landlords who forced peasants to grow indigo under exploitative terms, often leading to financial ruin for the farmers.
 
• **Zamindars** were local landlords who collected exorbitant taxes from peasants, often pushing them into extreme poverty.
 
• The movement aimed to protect peasants from these exploitative practices and assert their rights, under the guidance of Islamic principles.
 
• *The correct target of the campaign was **Indigo planters and zamindars**, making this option correct.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Faraizi Movement:**

 
 
• Founded by **Haji Shariatullah** in Bengal during the early 19th century (around 1819).
 
• The movement derived its name from “Farz,” which means obligatory duties in Islam. It advocated for the observance of Islamic principles and practices.
 
• It addressed both **religious and socio-economic oppression**, focusing on the plight of peasants and their exploitation by landlords and planters.
 
• The movement gained significant support among the Muslim peasantry in Bengal, who were economically and socially oppressed.
 
 
 
• **Indigo Planters:**
 
 
• Indigo cultivation in Bengal was introduced by the British during the colonial era.
 
• Planters forced farmers to grow indigo under exploitative contracts, often leading to **financial hardships** for the peasants.
 
• The cultivation of indigo was labor-intensive and reduced soil fertility, further worsening the conditions of the farmers.
 
• The exploitation of indigo farmers led to the historic **Indigo Revolt in 1859**, which was one of the first organized peasant movements in India.
 
 
 
• **Zamindari System:**
 
 
• The **Zamindari system** was introduced by the British in Bengal through the **Permanent Settlement Act of 1793**.
 
• Zamindars were given the role of collecting taxes from peasants on behalf of the British government.
 
• Many zamindars exploited peasants by collecting **exorbitant taxes** and seizing their lands in case of non-payment.
 
• The oppressive practices of zamindars were a major cause of rural poverty and led to widespread resentment among farmers.
 
 
 
• **Legacy of the Faraizi Movement:**
 
 
• It played a crucial role in raising awareness about the rights of peasants and resisting exploitation.
 
• The movement influenced later peasant uprisings such as the **Indigo Revolt** and other agrarian movements in colonial India.
 
• It also contributed to the socio-religious reform efforts among Muslims in Bengal.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• The **Indigo Revolt** of 1859 was a direct consequence of the exploitation of peasants by indigo planters and was a significant event in India’s struggle against colonial oppression.
 
• The movement under Haji Shariatullah also contributed to the development of Islamic reform movements in India, emphasizing the importance of socio-economic equality.
 
• The Faraizi Movement was not limited to religious reforms but also addressed the socio-political challenges faced by the Muslim peasantry in Bengal.
 
• Similar peasant movements during colonial times include the **Pagal Panthis** in Bengal and the **Deccan Riots** in Maharashtra.
 
• The role of religious leaders like Haji Shariatullah highlights how socio-economic struggles were often intertwined with religious reform during colonial India.
